explanations.explanation: Triumph, friend! Verse 1 says, "Clap your hands, all you peoples; shout unto God with a voice of triumph." That's not a polite little cough into your fist. That's the kind of shout that rattles the cooling racks, and I bet my mustache would be clapping right along.

I can see why a shout might sound sad to you, but this one isn't. Verse 1 says, "shout unto God with a voice of triumph." Triumph is the victory kind of shout, the kind you do when the whole batch comes out perfect. Mourning stays out of this verse completely.

A warning shout would be me yelling "Oven's hot!" across the bakery. That's not what this verse is doing. It says, "shout unto God with a voice of triumph." It's a celebration shout, and the whole crowd is invited.

All the earth, baker! Verse 2 says, "How awesome is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth!" Not one corner left out. Not even the corner of the earth where somebody still hasn't found their keys.

The seas are part of the earth, so that's a fair guess, but the psalm uses a bigger word. Verse 2 says, "How awesome is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth!" The psalm doesn't list the seas by name here. It just says all the earth.

I do love my night sky, so I get the pull of this one. But verse 2 says the LORD Most High is "…the great King over all the earth!" Stars don't show up in this line. The psalm keeps its eyes on the earth.
True! Verse 3 says, "He subdues nations beneath us, and peoples under our feet." The psalm is singing about what God does for His people. You can't beat that for a verse that starts with a victory.

This one is true. Verse 3 says, "He subdues nations beneath us, and peoples under our feet." So the psalm really does say God subdues nations beneath His people. Easy to doubt a line that big, friend, but it's right there in the text.
Close, but the psalm flips it. Verse 4 says, "He chooses our inheritance for us…" So God does the choosing, not the people. Think of it like a gift box that's already packed and handed to you.
False is right, baker! Verse 4 says, "He chooses our inheritance for us…" God does the choosing, not the people. Nobody is standing there with a clipboard picking their own.
He loves him! Verse 4 says, "He chooses our inheritance for us, the pride of Jacob, whom He loves." Love is the word the psalm uses. It sits right there in the verse.

Angry isn't in this verse, friend. Verse 4 says, "He chooses our inheritance for us, the pride of Jacob, whom He loves." The word the psalm uses for how He feels is love, and that's the opposite of angry. It's a good word, and it sits right next to the inheritance.

Grieved is a heavy word, and this verse doesn't use it. Verse 4 says, "…the pride of Jacob, whom He loves." Love is the feeling the psalm gives us here. I'd keep that one and leave the grieving out of it.
Shouts of joy, baker! Verse 5 says, "God has ascended amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn." Joy all around, and a horn blowing too. That's a sound I'd want to hear.
Fear doesn't show up in this verse. Verse 5 says, "God has ascended amid shouts of joy…" The sound around Him is joy, friend, and loud joy at that.
Mourning would be a slow, quiet song, and this verse is the opposite. It says, "God has ascended amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn." Shouts of joy, friend. Loud ones.

True! Verse 8 says, "God reigns over the nations; God is seated on His holy throne." The psalm gives us a picture of a King who is seated and reigning. That's the picture, baker, right there in the verse.

This one is true, baker. Verse 8 says, "God reigns over the nations; God is seated on His holy throne." So the psalm does picture God on His throne. It's a big picture, and I understand if it made you pause.

The God of Abraham! Verse 9 says the nobles "…have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham…" Abraham, the one Genesis 12 starts calling out of his homeland. The psalm ties this whole gathering back to that old family name.

Moses, the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, and I see why you reached for him. But verse 9 says the nobles "…have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham…" The psalm names Abraham here, not Moses.
Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36), but he isn't in this verse. Verse 9 says the nobles "…have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham…" Abraham is the name the psalm picks.

God, baker! Verse 9 says, "for the shields of the earth belong to God; He is highly exalted." The whole psalm has been saying He is King of all the earth, so this fits right in. Even the shields are His.
The nobles are in the verse, so I get it. But verse 9 says the nobles have assembled, and then, "for the shields of the earth belong to God…" The shields are God's, not theirs.

Israel's kings don't show up in this psalm at all. Verse 9 says, "for the shields of the earth belong to God; He is highly exalted." The shields belong to God. That fits a psalm that keeps calling Him King of all the earth.
